Structure-Aware Scientific Machine Learning for Personalized Digital Twins: From Personalized Biomedical Inference to Reliable Neural Network Solvers for Nonlinear PDEs

Chunyan Li

Postdoc, Department of Mathematics, University of South Carolina

Abstract

Understanding complex dynamical systems from sparse and heterogeneous data requires models that learn effectively while respecting the mathematical structures governing their evolution. In this talk, I present a structure-aware scientific machine learning research program spanning personalized biomedical inference and reliable neural solvers for nonlinear PDEs.

First, I introduce a personalized graph-PDE framework for characterizing the spatiotemporal progression of Alzheimer’s disease from longitudinal multimodal neuroimaging data such as MRI, PET, and resting-state fMRI. The model represents 68 brain regions as nodes in a patient-specific functional-connectivity graph and uses a low-rank representation to capture individual deviations from population-level connectivity. It couples amyloid-β, tau, neurodegeneration, and cognitive decline through local interactions and network-mediated propagation. To enable efficient parameter inference from sparse longitudinal data in this nonlinear model, I develop a hierarchical inference strategy and homotopy regularization. When applied to 1,891 participants from the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), the model improves the prediction of future biomarker and cognitive trajectories over homogeneous and standard clinical or neuroimaging benchmarks, with relative gains of up to 9.73% for individuals whose brain networks differ substantially from the population norm.

Second, scalable personalized mechanistic models require accurate and reliable forward simulation for nonlinear, multiscale PDEs. Using thermodynamically consistent phase-field systems as a testbed, I develop structure-aware neural network solvers that improve both where computational effort is allocated and how the neural network is optimized. Energy-dissipation-rate-guided adaptive sampling (EDRAS) targets regions with high local energy dissipation where interfacial evolution occurs, rather than refining solely where the PDE residual is large. For Allen–Cahn dynamics, EDRAS reduces relative mean-square error by up to a factor of six compared with residual-based refinement and identifies high-error regions more reliably. I also leverage random projection neural networks (RPNNs), which fix randomly generated hidden features and determine output coefficients via deterministic nonlinear least squares, enabling second-order optimization. I develop a structure-aware RPNN solver for the fourth-order Cahn–Hilliard system that combines a scaled auxiliary-variable formulation, separate random-feature spaces, adaptive sampling, and domain decomposition, achieving relative L² errors as low as 8.64 × 10⁻⁴ and outperforming matched deep-PINN baselines by nearly three orders of magnitude.

Together, these works advance interpretable, personalized mechanistic digital twins underpinned by reliable scientific machine learning.

About the speaker

Chunyan Li is a postdoctoral scholar in the Department of Mathematics at the University of South Carolina. Prior to this, she was a postdoctoral fellow at The Pennsylvania State University. She received her Ph.D. in Applied Mathematics from the University of South Carolina in December 2023. Her research lies at the intersection of applied mathematics, scientific machine learning, and biomedical modeling. She develops structure-aware, interpretable, and physics-consistent methods for complex dynamical systems, including personalized graph-PDE models of neurodegeneration and reliable neural-network solvers for nonlinear PDEs. Her ongoing work focuses on digital-twin frameworks for healthcare applications.
